title: Ordinal Numbers Grade 2: First to Twentieth (1st–20th) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Ordinal Numbers Grade 2: First to Twentieth Guide
meta_desc: Teach ordinal numbers grade 2 the easy way: first to twentieth, short forms like 1st and 2nd, the -th pattern, dates and races, plus a free quiz.
excerpt: Ordinals tell you position, not how many. Here is how I teach first to twentieth to seven-year-olds, the short-form pattern that trips them up, and a quick quiz to check it stuck.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Line up five children for a race and ask who came 3rd. Half the class will point at the third child; the other half will hold up three fingers. That mix-up — between which position and how many — is the whole reason ordinal numbers grade 2 matters. An ordinal number answers ‘where in the order?’ A cardinal number answers ‘how many?’ Getting a seven-year-old to feel that difference is the real lesson here, not the spelling of ‘twelfth’.

By the end of Grade 2 a child should read, write and use the ordinals from first to twentieth — 1st to 20th — and know when to reach for one instead of a counting number. Here is the order I teach it in, with the traps that actually catch children.

Ordinal versus cardinal: position, not quantity

Start concrete. Put four coins in a row. ‘How many coins?’ is four — that is cardinal. ‘Which coin is the shiny one?’ might be the second — that is ordinal. Same four coins, two different questions. I like to say cardinals count the group and ordinals point at one member of it.

The quickest way to make it stick is a queue at the water cooler. The child at the front is first, the next is second, and so on. Move one child and every position after them changes — that little shock is when the idea lands.

Writing ordinals in short form: 1st, 2nd, 3rd

Every ordinal has a two-letter tail stuck onto the number. The first three are the odd ones out, so teach them as a set to be memorised:

  • 1st — first
  • 2nd — second
  • 3rd — third

After that, life gets easy. From 4th onwards the tail is almost always -th: 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th, 10th. A useful shortcut for parents: the last two letters of the word written out are exactly the letters you tack on. ‘Fifth’ ends in th, so 5th. ‘Second’ ends in nd, so 2nd.

The -th pattern and its exceptions

Once a child trusts the -th rule, throw in the three that break it — because 21st, 22nd and 23rd will follow later and rest on the same idea. Within first to twentieth the tricky spellings are the ones to watch, not new tails. ‘Fifth’ drops a letter from five. ‘Eighth’ has just one t, not two. ‘Ninth’ loses the e from nine. And ‘twelfth’ swaps the ve of twelve for an f. These four are worth a little extra drill.

Ordinals on the calendar: reading dates

This is where ordinals earn their keep in real life. We say ‘the 15th of August’ and ‘my birthday is on the 9th’. A calendar is a grid of ordinals hiding as plain numbers. Point at the box marked 3 and ask ‘what is the date?’ — the answer, spoken aloud, is ‘the third’. Practising with real dates the family cares about — a festival, a birthday, the first of the month when pocket money arrives — makes ordinals feel useful rather than like a spelling test.

A quick game for position words

Read out a short list — mango, apple, banana, guava, litchi — and ask ‘which fruit is fourth?’ Then flip it: ‘guava is in which position?’ Going both ways, name to position and position to name, is what builds real fluency.

Positions in a race, a month and a queue

Ordinals show up everywhere a child already lives. In a race, runners finish first, second and third — that is where medals come from. In a month, the 1st is payday and the 26th is Republic Day. In a queue at the ration shop, being tenth in line is very different from being second. Whenever you catch one of these moments, name the ordinal out loud. Free, constant, real practice beats a worksheet you have to schedule.

One honest caveat from the classroom: do not rush the spellings. A child who can point to the 12th child in a line but writes ‘twelth’ is in far better shape than one who spells every ordinal perfectly yet cannot tell you who came third in the race. Understanding of position comes first; neat spelling follows.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz on exactly this — first to twentieth, short forms, and reading positions in a queue and a calendar. Let your child try it, then talk through anything they miss. When they are ready for written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has graded questions from matching to fill-in-the-blank, each with an answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 2 Ordinal Numbers Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on ordinal numbers from first to twentieth, short forms and positions. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 2 ordinal numbers, first to twentieth

questions.q: In the race Riya finished right after the winner. What position is Riya?
questions.explanation: The winner is 1st, so the runner right after is 2nd.

questions.q: What is the short form of ‘fifth’?
questions.explanation: From 4th onwards the tail is -th, so fifth is written 5th.

questions.q: Which word tells you a POSITION, not how many?
questions.explanation: Third is an ordinal — it names a place in order. The others count how many.

questions.q: Independence Day is on the 15th of August. How do we say ‘15th’?
questions.explanation: The ordinal for 15 is fifteenth, written 15th.

questions.q: Which short form is written correctly?
questions.explanation: Third ends in -rd, so it is written 3rd.

questions.q: There are 20 children in a line. What is the LAST child’s position?
questions.explanation: The ordinal for 20 is twentieth, written 20th.

questions.q: In the list mango, apple, banana, guava — which fruit is third?
questions.explanation: First mango, second apple, third banana. Banana is in third position.

questions.q: Which of these is spelt correctly?
questions.explanation: Eighth has just one t: eigh-th. So 8 in position is eighth, or 8th.

faq.q: What is the difference between ordinal and cardinal numbers?
faq.a: A cardinal number tells you how many — three apples. An ordinal number tells you the position in an order — the third apple in the row. Same objects, different question.

faq.q: Which ordinal short forms do not use -th?
faq.a: Only the first three: 1st (first), 2nd (second) and 3rd (third). From 4th all the way to 20th within Grade 2 the tail is -th.

faq.q: Which ordinal spellings do Grade 2 children get wrong most?
faq.a: Fifth, eighth, ninth and twelfth. ‘Eighth’ has one t, ‘ninth’ drops the e from nine, and ‘twelfth’ swaps the ve of twelve for an f. A little extra drill on these four helps.

faq.q: Where do children use ordinal numbers in real life?
faq.a: Dates on a calendar (the 9th of the month), positions in a race (first, second, third), and places in a queue. Naming these out loud as they happen is the best practice.
